lines.text: But perhaps all that I have been saying is only a matter of
fine phrases? Is such Christian existence, an existence in
both pain and sorrow, an existence which is no longer rooted
in this world, is it at all possible or is it merely a beautiful
fantasy? Is not the promise of resurrection from the dead a
perplexing and mysterious message for us?
Jesus anticipates such questions: "I have said this to you
in figures" or more precisely translated "in enigmas". For
to him who does not dare to believe, the promise is a
conundrum, a hollow sounding word. "The hour is coming
when I shall no longer speak to you in figures, but tell you
plainly of the Father." This does not mean that later Jesus
Will say something new and different from what He has
already said; it does mean that these puzzling words will
seem transparently clear and true. This is shown straight-
away by the remark of the disciples. Before Jesus says
anything different from what He has already said, namely
that He came from the Father and is returning to the Father,
they remark: "Ah, now you are speaking plainly, and not
in any figure!" The disciples speak thus from a faith which
anticipates the fulfilment of the promise.
And what is Jesus' reply? "Do you now believe? The
hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be
scattered..." Hence He appears to attach but little impor-
tance to the confession of faith. But no, we should not
understand it in that way! What we are to learn is rather
this: a quick impulsive confession of faith may mean very
little. Solid faith grows only in the experiences of life and
especially in the experience of despair. And to this experience
of despair the final word of His message applies: "I have said
this to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world
you have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome
the world."
This is no cheap word of comfort, as though Jesus' own
traversing of death and resurrection had spared us all
